sections.title: Prerequisite: The Bernoulli Trial
sections.content: Define a Bernoulli trial as an experiment with exactly two outcomes: Success (S) or Failure (F). Emphasize that probability p must remain constant.
sections.example: Visual animation: A coin flip. Heads (p=0.5) vs Tails (1-p=0.5).

sections.title: Defining the Binomial Conditions (BINS)
sections.content: Introduce the BINS acronym: Binary (two outcomes), Independent trials, Number of trials is fixed, Success probability is constant.
sections.example: Animated checklist showing a squirrel gathering nuts: Is it a success if it finds one? Are the tries independent? Yes!

sections.title: The Binomial Formula
sections.content: Present the formula: P(X=k) = C(n, k) * p^k * (1-p)^(n-k). Explain that C(n, k) calculates the number of ways to arrange 'k' successes in 'n' attempts.
sections.example: Visual tree diagram showing 3 flips of a coin, highlighting how many paths lead to exactly 2 Heads.

sections.title: Application: The Robot Scout
sections.content: Walk through a practical scenario. A robot scout has a 70% chance of successfully identifying a mineral. If it scans 5 sites, what is the probability it finds exactly 4?
sections.example: Step-by-step calculation: n=5, k=4, p=0.7. Show the probability distribution curve shifting as we solve it.

sections.title: Summary & Visualization
sections.content: Reiterate that the distribution shape depends on 'n' and 'p'. Preview how this predicts real-world likelihoods.
sections.example: An animated histogram morphing shape as 'p' changes from 0.1 to 0.5 to 0.9.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Bernoulli Trial
lecture_lines: A Bernoulli trial has two outcomes: Success or Failure.
The probability of success, p, must remain constant.
Think of flipping a coin: Heads is a success.
animations: Create a single circle (Coin) with color #FFD700.
Split the circle into two halves colored #FF4500 and #32CD32.
Add labels 'Success' (green) and 'Failure' (red) to the halves.
Flash the labels once to emphasize the binary outcome.

storyboard.title: Defining the Binomial Conditions (BINS)
lecture_lines: Use BINS to identify a binomial experiment.
Binary outcomes and Independent trials are essential.
Number of trials is fixed and p is constant.
animations: Display the acronym BINS using bold text in #FFFFFF.
Fade in bullet points for Binary, Independent, Number, Success.
Highlight each point with color #00CED1 as it appears.

storyboard.title: The Binomial Formula
lecture_lines: The Binomial formula calculates success probability.
It uses combinations to arrange successes in n trials.
P(X=k) accounts for successes and failures.
n is the number of trials.
k is the number of successes.
animations: Show the formula: P(X=k) = C(n,k) * p^k * (1-p)^(n-k).
Highlight the combination C(n,k) in color #FF69B4.
Highlight the probability term p^k * (1-p)^(n-k) in #7B68EE.

storyboard.title: Application: The Robot Scout
lecture_lines: Let's apply this to a Robot Scout.
Calculate the total probability for this outcome.
animations: Show a robot icon with text 'Scout' in #1E90FF.
Draw a path of 5 steps, highlighting successes in #32CD32.
Animate the robot moving successfully through 3 of 5 steps.

storyboard.title: Summary & Visualization
lecture_lines: Distribution shape depends on n and p.
Changing p morphs the histogram shape.
animations: Render a bar chart showing probabilities for 0 to 5 successes.
Highlight the highest probability bar with #FFD700.
Add a total probability label 'Sum = 1' in #FFFFFF.
